title: MA8-10787
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants are citizens of Burundi. XXX XXXXX (the male claimant) is 57 years old. His spouse, XXXX XXXXX (the female claimant), is 42 years old. Their three children are XXXX XXXX XXXX, 11 years old, XXXX XXXX XXXX, 9 years old, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, 6 years old.
The female claimant was appointed the designated representative for her three minor daughters.

The claimants arrived in Canada on April 9, 2007, and claimed refugee protection that day. They made the claim because they allege a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of their membership in a particular social group and their political opinion. They are also claiming refugee protection as persons in need of protection because they allege that they would be subjected to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, as well as to a danger of torture.
In his Personal Information Form (PIF), the male claimant alleges the following.
He is an ethnic Tutsi, born in northwest Burundi.

In November 1966, a captain from southern Burundi (Bururi) assumed power, and after that, Tutsis in the south discriminated against those in the north and, to a much greater extent, all Hutus in the country.
In 1971, non-southern army officers were charged and convicted for an attempted coup.
In 1972, Hutus were victims of a genocide, but hundreds of non-southern Tutsis were also killed.

The male claimant joined the army in 1973, at the invitation of the chief of staff. He was not aware of the army's involvement in the genocide, especially since the army had stopped going after Hutus at his school in XXXX.

The male claimant participated in XXXX XXXX in the USSR from 1973 to 1977 and again from 1987 to 1990. After achieving the rank of XXXX, he was subjected to discrimination because he was not a southern Tutsi. He was nevertheless promoted to XXXX in 1993.

The officers from the south attempted a coup on XXXX, 1993. Another attempt, on October 21, 1993, led to the assassination of President Ndadaye. The male claimant explained in his PIF how he opposed the rebels. He referred in particular to Exhibits P-281 and P-292 for information. He went to XXXX on XXXX, 1993, where he was arrested and detained for 21 months.

The male claimant was charged with the murder of President Ndadaye, but that charge was eventually withdrawn. Eighteen months after leaving for XXXX, he was charged with deserting the army and received a conditional six-month sentence. That sentence was appealed, and the Supreme Court proceedings have not yet been completed.

Upon his return to Burundi, the male claimant's statements caused him serious problems. In 1997, a grenade was thrown at his business. In 2001, he was arrested and detained for four hours. In 2003 or 2004, his taxes increased considerably. Finally, his application for a pardon was unsuccessful.

On XXXX, 2006, the male claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX: to explain that he had no role in the events of XXXX, 1993; to obtain a pardon; to press the Supreme Court to process his case; and to explain his position with respect to the coup. The male claimant took advantage of a change in the political environment to XXXX XXXX.

After the press conference, the male claimant received numerous threats, to the point that he realized that his and his family's lives were at risk. That is why he left his country and claimed refugee protection in Canada.
The male claimant's wife, XXXX XXXX, and his children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, base their claim on that of their husband and father.

The Minister alleges that the male claimant was a member of the Burundian army from 1976 [sic] to 1993 and that he had been promoted to the rank of XXXX. He also alleges that the Burundian army committed human and international rights violations and that the male claimant could have participated in or been complicit in crimes against humanity or acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations. He is therefore of the opinion that the male claimant should be excluded under articles 1F(a) and (c) of the Convention.
The panel determines that the male claimant, XXX XXXX, is not a refugee or a person in need of protection.
However, the female claimants, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are Convention refugees. 5. ANALYSIS 5.1 Identity
The claimants have valid identity documents, namely, passports issued by the Burundian authorities and several other documents. Their identities have therefore been established. 5.2 Testimony

The male claimant testified at length. His testimony contained no contradictions. He answered spontaneously and without hesitation. Moreover, much of his testimony was corroborated by an abundant amount of documentary evidence. However, as will be mentioned later on, the panel did not accept all of his statements. The female claimant XXXX XXXX testified briefly, and her testimony was credible. 5.3 Inclusion 5.3.1 Military career of the male claimant, XXX XXXX

Upon his arrival in Canada on April 9, 2007, the male claimant answered the questions of an immigration officer who questioned him, among other things, about his military career. The male claimant also addressed this topic in his response to question 31 of the PIF, and he added some details when he testified.

The male claimant joined the army in XXXX 1973, at the age of 20, at the invitation of the chief of staff at the time. He then began four years of training in the USSR. Up to the rank of XXXX, the male claimant, like his colleagues, was promoted regularly: he became a XXXX after six months, a XXXX XXXX XXXX after a year, and XXXX XXXX after two years. He returned to Burundi in 1977 and was promoted to XXXX in XXXX 1978. Finally, he became a XXXX in XXXX 1983.

The male claimant was a XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1979 and a XXXX XXXX in XXXX 1980. After a six-month stay in the USSR, from the end of 1982 to early 1983, the male claimant had XXXX XXXX XXXX. He returned to the USSR from 1987 to 1990. At the time, he was a XXXX-XXXX. Upon his return to the USSR, the male claimant was promoted to XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He then XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX. This was an XXXX-XXXX XXXX XXXX, the male claimant's specialty. After a failed coup in XXXX 1993, in which the male claimant was not involved, he was transferred to XXXX XXXX, where he had the same duties.

The male claimant stated that as a Tutsi from the northeast, he did not advance in his career as quickly as the southern Tutsis and that he had to protest to have this injustice corrected. Nevertheless, he was a XXXX - XXXX XXXX in 1990. 5.3.2 Progress of events following the attempted coup on October XX, 1993

In the presidential elections on June 1, 1993, and the parliamentary elections on June 29, 1993, the UPRONA party, which had led Burundi since 1965, lost to FRODEBU, a primarily Hutu party.3 Part of the Burundian army resisted the change and assisted with a first coup attempt on July 3, 1993. On October 21, 1993, during another coup attempt, the newly elected president, Melchior Ndadaye was assassinated along with some ministers and parliamentarians. It was in this context that the male claimant left Burundi on XXXX, 1993, and went to XXXX (now called the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX).

The male claimant's testimony about his role in the events on October 21 and 22, 1993, and his forced stay in XXXX is largely corroborated by the documentary evidence. In short, the first and eleventh battalions were behind the coup. The male claimant, who XXXX XXXX XXXX, went to XXXX at around 1:00 a.m. on October 21, 1993, in order to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Unfortunately, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, where XXXX XXXX was conducting operations. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who were to go to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
The male claimant stated that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He stated that his name was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX.

The panel is of the opinion that this statement is plausible and that the male claimant XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The male claimant talked XXXX XXXX. Note that he XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.4 The male claimant also XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006, and XXXX XXXX for this is on file.5 He submitted four accounts of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.6 He also submitted the DVD XXXX XXXX,7 and the panel notes that approximately XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
The panel notes that the male claimant XXXX XXXX of the XXXX on XXXX, 1993.

At 9:00 p.m. on October 21, 1993, a national public safety council broadcast the message that the coup had succeeded and that the entire army and police force had risen against the government. On October 22, the international community and Burundian civil society condemned the coup, to the extent that on October 23, Colonel Bikomagu read a news release on the radio and on television announcing that some parts of the armed forces had attempted a coup, but that the military command had ensured that constitutional legality would return.8

In the meantime, the male claimant fled Burundi at 10:00 a.m. on XXXX, 1993, to distance himself, according to him, from the coup attempt. He turned himself in to XXXX authorities and was placed under house arrest. From XXXX, he was transferred to XXXX, and on XXXX, 1993, he was transferred to XXXX and imprisoned. By coincidence, XXXX XXXX, XXXX of the coup attempt on July 3, 1993, and one XXXX XXXX coup on October 21, 1993, was also in Bukavu, as was his cousin XXXX, a XXXX XXXX. The documentation9 indicates that they left Burundi with help from the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The male claimant was detained in XXXX with these two individuals for 21 months.

The male claimant was detained at the request of the Burundian government, which had requested his extradition for complicity in the assassination of President Ndadaye. The other two detainees faced the same charge. Only the male claimant requested that he be returned to Burundi to face the charges. He made this request on XXXX, 1993.10 The list of letters that he sent to both XXXX and Burundian authorities in order to be repatriated to Burundi can be found in the article in the weekly newspaper XXXX.11

On XXXX, 1994, XXXX XXXX, Special Rapporteur for XXXX with the United Nations Commission on Human Rights, wrote a report specifically concerning the male claimant's case.12 He stated in particular that the male claimant wished to be returned to his country and concluded that the male claimant was being detained illegally and was a political prisoner. Despite this report, the male claimant continued to be held at the request of the Government of Burundi until XXXX, 1995.

The charge [translation] "of attempt on the life of a head of state" was withdrawn according to a letter from the Burundian minister of justice dated XXXX, 1995,13 but according to the male claimant, he was charged with desertion in XXXX 1995, that is, 18 months after his incarceration began.
There is no doubt that the male claimant's lengthy detention in XXXX constituted persecution.

Upon his return to Burundi in XXXX 1995, court martial proceedings for desertion began. On XXXX, 1996, the male claimant was convicted of desertion and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment.14 On XXXX, 1999, this sentence was upheld, but was suspended.15 This matter is still being appealed.

The male claimant did not seek to rejoin the army upon his return to Burundi in XXXX 1995. He lived with his brother until 1997, when he opened a XXXX. At that time, he started having a number of problems. In XXXX 1997, someone threw a grenade into his business, fortunately causing little damage. In 2000, a colonel threatened officers who frequented his XXXX. In 2001, he was arrested and detained for four hours. From 2002 to 2004, he experienced administrative problems. But it was following the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006, that his problems became very serious. 5.3.3 Press conference on XXXX, 2006

The male claimant explained that he had returned to Burundi to face his accusers, but stated that that he had been mistaken about the power structure and that several supporters of the coup on October 21, 1993, were still in power and had even been promoted.

The 1999 court martial decision was never legally served on him. The male claimant's lawyers had advised him not to request it. Since the political situation changed in 2006 and there was a new government and a new minister of justice, the male claimant felt it was a good time to relaunch his case. He requested that the 1999 decision be properly served on him, and the time frame for the appeal began from the moment it was served. It is in this context of political change and a new judicial remedy that the male claimant decided to publicly reopen his case. He wanted the right to have witnesses heard in his case, a right that had previously been denied. But, in particular, he wanted to rebuild his reputation, to testify about what he knew about the attempted coup on October 21, 1993, and to state publicly that he had never been involved in the conspiracy.

The DVD of XXXX 16 confirms that the male claimant talked with some freedom and even with a hint of provocation, naming soldiers involved in the coup who had been promoted. 5.3.4 Consequences of preceding events

Once again, it seems that the male claimant perhaps miscalculated the risks that he was taking. After the conference, the male claimant received a series of threatening calls on his cellphone. Some calls were even made to his fixed-line telephone, which the female claimant answered. He was called a traitor. He was accused of being a member of FRODEBU and a perpetrator of genocide. These anonymous calls were made frequently after the press conference.

In XXXX 2007, during an anonymous call, the caller referred to a friend who had been killed in 1995 or 1996. Because of that threat, the male claimant decided to apply for a visa for the United States. On XXXX, 2007, someone punctured his tires, broke a window and the rear-view mirror, and left a message: [translation] "Remember that you have a wife and children".
Knowing that it would be difficult for him to cross the border, a friend provided him with trustworthy soldiers to help him.

The claimants come from a country where 250,000 people have been killed since 1993.17 There is a serious possibility, as the male claimant stated at the hearing, that he or his family would be attacked under the cover of generalized violence. The economic power still belongs to the Tutsis, especially those from Bururi, those whom the male claimant targeted in his accusations. His fear is well founded by reason of his political opinion. Ward18 defines political opinion as any opinion on any matter in which the machinery of state, government and policy may be engaged. This is the case for the male claimant. As for his family, which was directly targeted by the threats, their fear is based on their membership in a particular social group, the family. Their fear is also well founded.

Given the reputation of the people whom the male claimant attacked and their connection with political structure, the claimants cannot expect to receive adequate state protection or find refuge in the small country of Burundi. 5.4 Exclusion 5.4.1 Introduction

The Minister intervened to have the male claimant, XXX XXXX, excluded from the protection that could be granted to him under the Act. A similar request was not made for the other claimants. 5.4.2 The Act

Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act19 (the Act) define the terms "refugee" and "person in need of protection". Section 98 of the Act reads as follows: 98. A person referred to in section E or F of Article 1 of the Refugee Convention is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

Sections E and F of the Convention have been incorporated into the Act. In this case, section F of article 1 of the Convention is relevant. It reads as follows: F. The provisions of this Convention shall not apply to any person with respect to whom there are serious reasons for considering that: (a) he has committed a crime against peace, a war crime, or a crime against humanity, as defined in the international instruments drawn up to make provision in respect of such crimes; (b) he has committed a serious non-political crime outside the country of refuge prior to his admission to that country as a refugee; (c) he has been guilty of acts contrary to the purposes and principles of the United Nations.
As section F indicates, there must be serious reasons for considering that the crimes mentioned were committed or that the acts specified were carried out.

The burden is on the Minister to prove that the male claimant falls within the category of excluded persons. Counsel for the Minister did not claim that the male claimant himself had directly committed crimes against humanity. However, he claimed that because of the position that he held, he must be considered an accomplice in crimes committed by the regime in power from 1973 to 1993. 5.4.3 Case law

De Montigny J., in Pineda Collins v. M.C.I.,20 summarizes the principles previously established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Ramirez,21 Moreno22 and Sivakumar.23 He first cites an excerpt from Zazai and then makes several additional comments. This analysis is very complete, and it is worthwhile to reproduce it here in its entirety: [22] My colleague Justice Layden-Stevenson has aptly summarized the principles governing the required level of participation to establish complicity, and I cannot do better but to quote from her decision in Zazai v. Canada (MCI), [2004] F.C.J. 1649: [27] Accomplices as well as principal actors may be found to have committed international crimes (although, for present purposes, I am not concerned with principal actors). The court accepted the notion of complicity defined as a personal and knowing participation in Ramirez and complicity through association whereby individuals may be rendered responsible for the acts of others because of their close association with the principal actors in Sivakumar. Complicity rests on the existence of a shared common purpose and the knowledge that all of the parties may have of it: Ramirez; Moreno. [28] Madam Justice Reed in Penate v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 2 F.C. 79 (T.D.) synthesized the trilogy principles at pages 84 and 85: The Ramirez, Moreno, and Sivakumar cases all deal with the degree or type of participation which will constitute complicity. Those cases have established that mere membership in an organization which from time to time commits international offences is not normally sufficient to bring one into the category of an accomplice. At the same time, if the organization is principally directed to a limited, brutal purpose, such as a secret police activity, mere membership may indeed meet the requirements of personal and knowing participation. The cases also establish that mere presence at the scene of an offence, for example, as a bystander with no intrinsic connection with the persecuting group will not amount to personal involvement. Physical presence together with other factors may however qualify as a personal and knowing participation. As I understand the jurisprudence, it is that a person who is a member of the persecuting group and who has knowledge that activities are being committed by the group and who neither takes steps to prevent them from occurring (if he has the power to do so) nor disengages himself from the group at the earliest opportunity (consistent with safety for himself) but who lends his active support to the group will be considered to be an accomplice. A shared common purpose will be considered to exist. I note that the situation envisaged by this jurisprudence is not one in which isolated incidents of international offences have occurred but where the commission of such offences is a continuous and regular part of the operation. [23] It is clear from the foregoing that to be found complicit in crimes against humanity, a claimant has to have the required mental element for complicity. If the organization with which the claimant is associated is one dedicated to a "limited, brutal purpose", then the required mental element is inferred from the claimant's "mere membership" in the organization. This was clearly not the case here, as the Board found that the Mexican army is not such an organization. [24] The mental element required to establish complicity in crimes against humanity has been characterized variously as "shared common purpose", "personal and knowing participation or toleration of the crimes", and participation in an organization knowing it commits crimes against humanity, when combined with a failure to stop the crimes or disassociate oneself. [25] Also implicit in the notion of "guilty knowledge" is proportionality. Those in leadership positions must bear more moral responsibility for crimes committed by their organizations than non-leaders. As Justice Tremblay-Lamer stated in Zrig v. Canada (MCI), [2002] 1 F.C. 559, at para. 99, quoting from Nadon J. in Mohammad v. Canada (MCI), (1995), 115 F.T.R. 161: The more important the position held by a person in an organization that has committed one or more crimes, the more likely his or her complicity. A person who continues to hold a leadership position in such an organization with full knowledge that the organization is responsible for crimes may be considered an accomplice. [26] Finally, passive acquiescence will not be sufficient to establish a basis for exclusion. As indicated in Moreno v. Canada (MCI), [1994] 1 F.C. 298 (F.C.A.), personal involvement in the persecutorial acts must be established in order to demonstrate complicity. 5.4.4 Documentary evidence concerning the Burundian army from 1965 to 1993

The male claimant was a member of the Burundian army for 20 years, from 1973 to 1993. Numerous documents entered on the record show the army's complete domination by the Tutsi ethnic group during that period (and before) and the extremely serious human rights violations of which the army was guilty.

It is important to mention the events that happened before the male claimant joined the army in 1973, although what happened before 1973 cannot be held against him. The Minority Rights Group International report published in March 199524 provides a good summary of this first period. This report was written by a renowned specialist in the region, Filip Reyntjens. The introduction reads as follows: In the particular Burundian context, a short comment on the concept of minority/majority is called for. As the Hutu constitute a large demographic majority (80-85 per cent), the Tutsi (15-20 per cent) and the Twa (under 1 per cent) would be expected to be the main concern of MRG. However, the Tutsi have dominated politics, the army, the civil service, education and the economy; and up to the massacres of late 1993, the Hutu were by far the most numerous victims of ethnic-political violence. With the exception of the short period of democratic rule between 10 July and 21 October 1993, the Tutsi - or, more accurately, a small Tutsi élite - have thus been dominant, despite constituting a demographic minority.25

Reyntjens then explains that in 1965, a failed coup was violently repressed. The entire Hutu political elite was killed, which ended all Hutu political involvement for many years,26 and between 2,500 and 5,000 people died.27

In 1972, another attempted coup was followed by the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus and the exile of another 300,000. There were almost no Hutus left in the army. No one was prosecuted for this genocide.28

In November 1976, Colonel Bagaza overturned the Micombero regime-both parties were southern Tutsis-and the army remained a major force. From 1984 to 1987, the human rights situation seriously deteriorated, with a considerable increase in the number of political prisoners. Pierre Buyoya, another southern Tutsi, came to power in September 1987, following a coup. The army continued to be dominated by the Tutsi-Hima elite (from the south), and the Hutus continued to be discriminated against and prosecuted.29
The preceding events, specifically, of course, the massacre of 100,000 to 200,000 Hutus in 1972, are corroborated by many of the documents entered on the record.

In 1988, the Burundian army was almost entirely made up of Tutsis, who constituted 99.7% of the force.30 In August of that year, Hutu gangs massacred hundreds of Tutsis in the communes of Ntega and Marangara, in northern Burundi. The army re-established order, and in the following week, massacred approximately 20,000 Hutus, most of whom were not involved in the incidents. In addition, 60,000 Hutus fled to Rwanda. The government admitted that 5,000 people had died, but did not take responsibility.31

This is how Reyntjens described the situation in L'Afrique des Grands Lacs en crise [the Great Lakes Region of Africa in crisis]:32 [translation] When the army intervened on August 17, it used the "steamroller" system, which had proven successful in 1972. Since the Tutsis had fled to neighbouring communes, the army shot at anything that moved. Helicopters were used for massive strafing and for launching incendiary grenades. According to an Amnesty International report, the soldiers' conduct proves "that their orders were not only to put an end to the disorder, but also to carry out mass executions of members of the Hutu community.... The troops were engaged ... in a repression of the entire Hutu civilian population aimed at punishing them and killing them, rather than at restoring order." Code Cissé, the representative in Rwanda of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, said, "This is no longer a civil war, because only one side has weapons. It has become a massacre by the Burundian army." The indiscriminate nature of the repression is evidenced by the many women and children who were victims of the military action. Here again, the count is difficult to establish. The government's claim that there were 5,000 victims is clearly far from reality, and various sources estimate that as many as 20,000 people, mostly Hutus, have been killed. In addition, nearby Rwanda has taken in approximately 60,000 refugees, primarily in the prefecture of Butare.
The facts relating to this massacre in August 1988 are reported in other documents entered on the record.33

Pressed by the international community, Buyoya implemented significant changes and began to integrate Hutus into public institutions. However, the army resisted the change. Buyoya's message did not go over well in the military establishments, which is reflected in the events of November 1991.34

On November 23, 1991, poorly armed Hutu militants attacked a police station in XXXX and a military post in the province of Cibitoke. The army's retaliation caused the deaths of more than 1,000 people, according to the various reports. The government admitted that 500 people died.35

This documentary evidence leaves no doubt that the Burundian army committed, over numerous years, crimes against humanity. This evidence comes from key international human rights monitors and is not contradicted. The panel finds it to be credible and trustworthy.

Mugesera v. Canada36 defines crime against humanity as follows: 119 As we shall see, based on the provisions of the Criminal Code and the principles of international law, a criminal act rises to the level of a crime against humanity when four elements are made out: 1. An enumerated proscribed act was committed (this involves showing that the accused committed the criminal act and had the requisite guilty state of mind for the underlying act); 2. The act was committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack; 3. The attack was directed against any civilian population or any identifiable group of persons; and 4. The person committing the proscribed act knew of the attack and knew or took the risk that his or her act comprised a part of that attack.

Murder is clearly a proscribed act and meets the first criterion. When the victims are in the thousands, it must be concluded that the attack is necessarily a systematic attack at the least. The second criterion is therefore met. The third criterion requires that the attack be directed against a civilian population or an identified group; the documentary evidence shows that the Hutu civilian population was the victim of attacks by the army for years. Finally, the person, that is, the Burundian army, was aware of the context of the attack. That also goes without saying.
The panel therefore concludes that in 1965, 1972, 1988 and 1991, the Burundian army committed crimes against humanity against the Hutu civilian population.

However, the Minister did not allege that the Burundian army was an organization directed toward a limited and brutal purpose. In fact, it certainly had other functions. 5.4.5 The facts concerning the male claimant

The Minister also did not allege that the male claimant had participated personally in any massacres. Rather, he alleged that it was as a member of the army that he was complicit in crimes against humanity committed by the Burundian army. Therefore, he was allegedly complicit by association in the crimes. The male claimant primarily argued that he was not aware of the crimes committed by the Burundian army and that, ultimately, he dissociated himself from it.

On the last point, the panel notes a significant confusion in this argument. The male claimant might have dissociated himself from the army in 1993, but he allegedly dissociated himself because of those who had attempted the coup. His dissociation had nothing to do with the crimes committed by the army previously, when the male claimant was not only a member of the army, but also a member of XXXX XXXX.

As for his knowledge of the crimes committed by the army, the male claimant alleged that information was not circulating and that he did not know what was going on. The panel finds that this statement is not credible. First, it is contradicted in his own PIF and in XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2006.

The male claimant wrote in his PIF that he did not consider in 1973, when he was 20 years old, the army's involvement in the genocide. The 1972 genocide was preceded in 1965 by the massacre of the Hutu political elite. There were allegedly between 2,500 and 5,000 deaths, and 300,000 people were exiled. This could not have been unknown, even by a young man of 20. As for the 1972 genocide, during which 100,000 to 200,000 people were killed, in part by the army, it is impossible that the male claimant did not know this fact at the time he joined the army.

In his response to question 31 of his PIF, in the second paragraph on page 1, the male claimant spoke of the power that the southern Tutsis had in 1966 and of the discrimination against all other Tutsis at the time. He added as follows: [translation] Of course, the Hutus continued to be subjected to the most segregation, when they were not simply physically eliminated.
Nevertheless, some northern Tutsis held high-ranking positions. For example, the chief of staff who helped the male claimant become a soldier was from the north.

In his PIF, the male claimant also stated37 that the army has always been the main supporter of the authoritarian regimes and the perpetrators of the coups. Finally, still according to his PIF,38 the male claimant called the army "la grande muette" [the great silent one], implying that army members did not speak, but that does not mean that they did not know anything.

In the press release of XXXX, 2006,39 the male claimant wrote the following: [translation] The lesson was learned in 1972; I XXXX and a student at the Collège du XXXX XXXX. Hundreds of thousands of innocent human lives were taken by the war. I was a powerless witness to this tragedy.
The panel concludes from all of this that the male claimant must have had a good idea of the army's role in the massacres in 1965 and 1972 when he joined the army in 1973.

As for the 1988 massacre (nearly 20,000 people died during the army's reprisals), the male claimant stated that, when he was in the USSR, he had heard rumours that the army had committed some blunders. The panel cannot believe that the male claimant knew nothing else, when he was already a XXXX-XXXX.

The massacre in November 1991 took place in the province of Cibitoke and in XXXX. It is impossible that the male claimant, who XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX and who had the rank XXXX, knew very little about this, especially since the government had admitted that 500 people had died.
Consequently, the panel concludes that the male claimant was aware of the crimes against humanity committed by the Burundian army when he was a member.

As de Montigny J. stated in Pineda Collins v. M.C.I.,40 there is complicity when there is "participation in an organization knowing it commits crimes against humanity, when combined with a failure to stop the crimes or disassociate oneself". It is not certain that the male claimant had enough influence to oppose the army's actions. Regardless, he did not try to dissociate himself. The male claimant stated that he knew only one colleague who had resigned, and that person suffered economic hardship as a result because of an order preventing him from being hired without the army's authorization. The panel is of the opinion that these problems did not affect his safety and could not be a valid reason for the male claimant to maintain his association with the army. The panel is therefore of the opinion that the male claimant could have left the army well before 1993.

Finally, the male claimant had a very XXXX XXXX within the army. The panel highlights again the words of de Montigny J. in Pineda Collins v. M.C.I.:41 [25] Also implicit in the notion of "guilty knowledge" is proportionality. Those in leadership positions must bear more moral responsibility for crimes committed by their organizations than non-leaders. As Justice Tremblay-Lamer stated in Zrig v. Canada (MCI), [2002] 1 F.C. 559, at para. 99, quoting from Nadon J. in Mohammad v. Canada (MCI), (1995), 115 F.T.R. 161: The more important the position held by a person in an organization that has committed one or more crimes, the more likely his or her complicity. A person who continues to hold a leadership position in such an organization with full knowledge that the organization is responsible for crimes may be considered an accomplice.

For all of these reasons, the panel is of the opinion that there are serious reasons for considering that the male claimant committed a crime against humanity and must be excluded from the protection that can be granted under the Act.

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel determines that the male claimant, XXX XXXX, is a person referred to in article 1F(a) of the Convention. Consequently, as required by section 98 of the Act, the male claimant cannot be considered a refugee or a person in need of protection.

As for the female claimants XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, they have satisfactorily discharged their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on one of the grounds set out in the Convention, that is, their membership in a particular social group. Consequently, they are Convention refugees in accordance with section 96 of the Act.
